extracted.intended_audience: researchers/authors submitting health-related preprints to medRxiv
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria that medRxiv uses to screen submitted manuscripts for scope, ethical oversight, patient-identifying information, trial registration, originality, and potential public harm before posting as preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission completeness / metadata accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house screening staff with scientific and editorial expertise check that the details inputted during submission are complete - e.g., the authors have included the appropriate information in the submission fields, special characters are coded correctly, and any group authors are not incorrectly listed as individual authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screeners verify submission-field completeness and correct encoding/formatting; incomplete or incorrect metadata may delay handling. Examples given: author information, special characters, group authorship formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and article type acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The in-house screeners ensure the manuscript itself is within scope and an appropriate article type: a research manuscript or clinical research design protocol is acceptable; a narrative review, commentary, opinion piece, or a case report/case series is not (a full list of appropriate article types can be found in our FAQ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should confirm their manuscript is an acceptable article type per medRxiv FAQ; out-of-scope article types are grounds for flagging or rejection/escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical oversight declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate details of ethical oversight approval/exemption by an independent entity dedicated to the ethical oversight of research studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts lacking an adequate ethics declaration may be escalated for discussion and could be delayed or declined. Include documentation of approval or exemption as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of participant/patient identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that could potentially identify patients or research participants (e.g., photographs, exact age, location, identifying medical conditions, travel histories, family relationship identifiers, or identifying pedigree data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions containing potentially identifying information are flagged; authors should remove or anonymize identifying details to avoid escalation. Examples of identifying material are provided to guide authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial registration / presence of clinical trial ID
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a clinical trial ID for clinical or educational interventions. We deem a clinical trial to be any research project that prospectively assigns people or a group of people to an intervention, with or without concurrent comparison or control groups, to study the relationship between a health-related intervention and a health outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a clinical trial is unregistered or lacks a recognized registry ID, the submission can be escalated. Authors of prospectively assigned intervention studies should include the trial registry identifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and prior-publication screening (automated text analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions also undergo automated text analyses to identify potential plagiarism and/or material that has already appeared online (e.g., in a journal or on another preprint server).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should ensure originality and disclose prior publication; automated checks may flag overlap with published or online material and prompt further action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health-related research determination by Affiliates
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliates consider: Does the manuscript present health-related research (i.e. is it a clinical research manuscript that includes methods and data)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volunteer clinicians and health professionals assess whether the submission is clinical research (methods and data); if deemed not health-related research, the submission is flagged for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of potential for public harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Affiliates consider: Is there potential for public harm from posting it as a preprint?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content or conclusions may cause harm to the public (e.g., might encourage reduced compliance with critical public health measures), the manuscript is escalated for further review and may not be posted without resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript escalation and further review triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts can be escalated at any stage in the screening process for discussion by the Content Team and, where needed, the medRxiv Founders and individual Affiliates or external advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of escalation reasons include: article type or content not in scope; missing appropriate ethics declaration; manuscript contains potentially identifying information; clinical trial not registered in a recognized registry; manuscript contains content/conclusions that may cause public harm. Escalation means additional discussion and possible decisions beyond routine screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, processing time, and posting policy (no embargo/scheduled posting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The screening process typically takes 2–4 days, but can take longer over weekends and holidays, or if the submission requires in-house discussion and further correspondence with authors. Authors should note that manuscripts cannot be posted at a specific date or time, or their release embargoed according to a requested schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should plan for a multi-day screening window and cannot request a specific posting date/time or embargoed release; delays may occur if escalation or author correspondence is required.
